# choosewise.education

> An independent education resource on AI in schools, built and edited by Johan Lindström — a Swedish education consultant with 28 years in the school system (10 as teacher, 7 as school leader, 11 in EdTech). The site offers a four-step decision framework (WISE), downloadable prompt packs by role and subject, curated infographic styles for Gemini Notebook, and interactive AI-or-human tests. Content is published in English and Swedish; the Swedish surface uses the parallel name RÄTT-modellen.

The site's thesis: schools usually don't need more AI tools — they need the judgment to choose the right tool at the right time. Material is written for principals, school administrators (skolchefer), and teachers, and aims to be practical, evidence-aware, and free of vendor hype.

## The WISE Framework for Education

- [The WISE Framework for Education (English)](https://choosewise.education/wise/): Four-step decision model — Weigh the learning goal, Inspect what the subject requires, Select the right tool, Evaluate the outcome — for choosing AI tools in school settings.
- [RÄTT-modellen (Swedish)](https://choosewise.education/sv/ratt/): Same framework, Swedish surface and language.

## Prompt Packs

Free downloadable PDFs of ready-to-use AI chat prompts, organized by role and subject. Indices:

- [All prompts — English](https://choosewise.education/prompts/)
- [Alla promptar — Svenska](https://choosewise.education/sv/promptar/)

Sample role-based packs: Teachers, Principals, School administrators, District administrators, Superintendents, Lead teachers, EdTech coaches, Education strategists, School counselors, School psychologists, School nurses, School librarians, Special education specialists/teachers, Student assistants, Career counselors, School caretakers, School catering staff, School IT managers, District IT managers.

Sample subject-based packs (compulsory + upper secondary): Art, Biology, Chemistry, Crafts, Cross-curricular work, Digital tools, Early numeracy, English, Geography, History, Home economics, Mathematics, Modern languages, Music, Outdoor education, Physical education, Physics, Preschool, Reception, Religious studies, Science, Social studies, Technology, Time management, Learning new skills, Research on learning, Megaprompts (#1, #2, #3).

## AI or human?

- [AI or human? — English](https://choosewise.education/ai-or-human/)
- [AI eller människa? — Svenska](https://choosewise.education/sv/ai-eller-manniska/)

Interactive tests where visitors check whether they can tell AI-generated text, images, and video apart from human-created content.

## Infographic Styles

- [Infographic styles (140) — English](https://choosewise.education/infographic-styles/)
- [Infografik-stilar (140) — Svenska](https://choosewise.education/sv/infografik-stilar/)

A curated catalogue of 140 visual styles (with prompts) for generating Gemini Notebook video overviews and slide decks.

## Visual Codes

- [50 visual codes for ChatGPT — English](https://choosewise.education/visual-codes/)

Fifty one-word, slash-prefixed prompts (such as /cutaway, /anatomy, /ghosted) that turn an uploaded photo into a teaching visual in ChatGPT. Sorted into eight categories; every code is demonstrated with a draggable before/after slider on the same photo, and the page explains how to make your own.

- [Visual codes for video — English](https://choosewise.education/visual-codes/video/)

One-word codes for AI video: send a start image with a code such as /timelapse, /xray or /lightshift and get a five-second clip. Codes with classroom value (science processes, change over time, film language for art class) and for everyday use, each shown as start image and finished clip with the exact prompt. Codes that failed in testing are listed with what went wrong, and clips with factual errors are marked as "spot the error" material.

- [Visual codes for studying — English](https://choosewise.education/visual-codes/study/)

Codes such as /cheatsheet, /quizmate or /flashcards that, typed into an AI chatbot with a topic and "Make it an image", return a study poster or a worksheet. 27 codes tested on photosynthesis, the French Revolution and the Pythagorean theorem. Part 1 holds the codes that make students practise (each needs one added sentence, shown on its card); Part 2 the posters to read, each with a way to make reading active. The page explains that the codes are not official commands but the model's average reading of the word, documents the factual errors and weak answer keys found in testing, and lists four codes that failed.

## Think + AI

- [Think + AI — English](https://choosewise.education/think/)

Free tools that help teachers of Grades 8–12 train students' thinking when AI makes answers cheap. AI does the preparation on the teacher's side; students do the thinking, mostly without a screen.

- [Thinking Moves — English](https://choosewise.education/thinking-moves/)

Twelve five-minute thinking tasks (such as Best explanation, Check the claim, Then what? and Think back) grouped into six clusters of thinking. A prompt builder turns a subject, topic and grade into a prompt for any AI tool; each move has two worked examples from different subjects and an evidence label (Strong, Promising or Framework) that rates research on teaching that kind of thinking regularly. A free PDF card deck includes a fill-in prompt for offline use.

- [Flawed Answer — English](https://choosewise.education/flawed-answer/)

A fifteen-minute task for Grades 8–12. The teacher uses any AI tool to write a confident answer about the lesson topic that contains exactly one error of reasoning, of one of six types (wrong cause, correlation as cause, missing step, overgeneralisation, hidden assumption, right answer for the wrong reason), at one of two difficulty levels. Students are told an AI wrote it and, in pairs, find the flaw, fix it, explain why it convinces and say how they would test it. Six worked examples with teacher keys, an upper-secondary variant, a one-page student frame and a PDF card deck.

- [Side by Side — English](https://choosewise.education/side-by-side/)

A fifteen-minute comparison task for Grades 7–12. The teacher uses any AI tool to build two items placed side by side, of one of five pair types (two ways to the same answer, right next to wrong, one thing changed, two concepts that are easily confused, two sources on the same event), at one of two difficulty levels. The AI reply has a block for students and a separate teacher key. Students sort what is only in A, in both and only in B, write the rule they found and try it on a new case C. Five worked examples shown as real pairs, evidence labels, an upper-secondary variant, a one-page student sheet and a PDF card deck.

- [Thinking Profile — English](https://choosewise.education/thinking-profile/)

A planning tool for a whole unit built around one kind of thinking, practised in four to six tasks. Six clusters of thinking (generating ideas, evaluating and choosing, comparing and transferring, explaining and reasoning from basics, causes and systems, regulating your own thinking), each with a four-step ladder students use to check their own progress. A planning prompt builds on Thinking Moves, Flawed Answer and Side by Side and returns a unit plan for any AI tool, plus free PDFs.

## Pedagogy + AI

- [Pedagogy + AI — English](https://choosewise.education/pedagogy/)

Free tools that bring learning research into the lessons teachers of Grades 6–12 already plan, with any AI tool. The teacher keeps their lesson and their way of teaching; the research works in the background.

- [Lesson Lens — English](https://choosewise.education/lesson-lens/)

The teacher pastes a lesson they have already planned and picks one or two of twelve research lenses (such as Retrieval practice, Cognitive load and worked examples, Formative check, Feedback, Explicit instruction, Metacognition and the trade-off question about AI use). Formative check is the suggested starting lens. A prompt builder returns a prompt for any AI tool, and the answer always comes in four parts: Keep (what already works), Upgrade (at most two concrete changes), Nudge (a question, only when research points to a stronger option) and Check (what to look for in class). Each lens has a worked example, an evidence label (Strong, Promising, Framework or Choosewise) and a link to the Evidence Toolkit. A free PDF card deck includes a fill-in prompt for offline use.

- [Retrieval Rhythm — English](https://choosewise.education/retrieval-rhythm/)

A weekly routine for retrieval practice and spacing. The teacher keeps a simple topic log (date, topic, key points; an Excel template is provided) and once a week pastes it into a prompt builder. Any AI tool then returns one starter per lesson that mixes content from the newest week in the log, one to three weeks before it and older entries, in one of five formats (starter quiz, brain dump, retrieval grid, multiple choice with misconceptions, two things I remember) or a mix, with an answer key and a list of answers to verify. Evidence labels for retrieval practice and spacing (Strong) and interleaving and misconception-based options (Promising). A free printable pack has the five formats, a page for students and parents and a fill-in prompt.

- [Two-Minute Debrief — English](https://choosewise.education/two-minute-debrief/)

For the lessons that didn't go as planned. The teacher answers four questions (goal, evidence, surprise, next) and a prompt builder returns a prompt for any AI tool. The answer comes in four parts: two likely causes tied to the lesson's content, one concrete move for the next lesson with minutes, a check written for students with a threshold for moving on, and one question back to the teacher. The check result becomes the evidence in the next debrief for that group. Debriefs can be saved in the teacher's own browser for an end-of-day prompt and a weekly roll-up that finds patterns across lessons. Includes four exit ticket templates (with Microsoft Forms and Google Forms setup), an Excel unit journal and a free printable pack. Evidence labels for formative assessment, feedback and worked examples (Strong), and hinge questions and structured teacher reflection (Framework).

## Study + AI

- [Study + AI — English](https://choosewise.education/study/)

Free tools that help students in Grades 7–12 study in ways research shows work, with or without AI. Teachers can prepare the material with AI; students do the studying.

- [Study Moves — English](https://choosewise.education/study-moves/)

Ten study moves for students in Grades 7–12, chosen by goal: remember it, tell similar things apart, understand it, solve problems, fix your mistakes and start a new topic. The moves are Test yourself (retrieval practice, the suggested starting move), Spread it out (spaced practice), Mix it up (interleaving), Explain it simply (the Feynman technique), Ask why (elaborative interrogation), Draw it (dual coding), Find an example (concrete examples), Study a solved example (worked examples), Fix your mistakes (feedback) and Guess first (pretesting). Every move is complete without AI, with steps, a worked example, a note on why it feels harder than re-reading, an evidence label (Strong, Promising or Framework) and sources. A prompt builder has two versions: a teacher prepares printable study material with any AI tool, or a student aged 13 and over gets a study partner that asks one question at a time, never gives the answer before the student has tried and never writes homework. Includes AI age rules and a free PDF card deck with fill-in prompts for teachers and students.

- [The Study Experiment — English](https://choosewise.education/study-experiment/)

A free two-lesson classroom kit for Grades 7–12, a school version of a demonstration used with university classes (Einstein, Mullet & Harrison 2012). Every student studies two short texts, one by reading it twice and one by writing down what they remember and then checking, with the two groups counterbalanced. Students predict which text they will remember better, and an unannounced quiz a week later shows the class's own result. A results view in the browser compares prediction with outcome without saving anything. Lesson 2 includes discussion questions, a three-point explanation, a script for an even result and a concrete study plan for each student. A prompt builder helps the teacher make the two texts and the quiz with any AI tool; students do not use AI. Includes AI age rules and a free PDF teacher kit with group cards, anonymous slips and a fill-in prompt.

- [Test Countdown — English](https://choosewise.education/test-countdown/)

A free study planner for students in Grades 7–12. The student types the test date, what the test covers (one to six areas), the session length and the days they can study, and gets short dated sessions on different days within the last three weeks before the test: a quiz on each area that brings earlier areas back, mixed quizzes, a practice test near the end and a short last session. Every session works with the notes closed and needs no AI. When there are only a few study days the plan is shorter and says that less time means less will stay with the student. The plan is made in the browser and lives in the link, so it can be bookmarked, shared with a whole class or printed; nothing is saved or sent. Includes how to quiz yourself, why the sessions feel harder than rereading, the research behind the plan, a prompt builder with which a teacher makes the quizzes with any AI tool, and AI age rules.
